name: Deep Cerise
lede: Deep Cerise darkens cerise, the French word for cherry, into a strong purplish red that our archive has caught in oil paint exactly once.

sections.title: Cherry, made deeper
sections.body:
Cerise is simply the French word for cherry, and the OED's first English citation for it as a color word is 1858, in *The Times* [1]. Deep Cerise adds the usual darkening modifier on top of [[cerise]] [1]. Wikipedia's source for this exact shade is Crayola, which places it among the commercial, catalog-born names rather than the older dye or dictionary tradition [2].

The ISCC-NBS system of 1955 classifies it as a strong purplish red, and its nearest named neighbor in our library is [[mulberry]], 4.3 CIEDE2000 units away [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds Deep Cerise in exactly 1 of 23,781 paintings, as photographed, rarer than 86 percent of the named colors we track [4]. In printed English the word's all-sense use peaks in the 1910s, decades before the Crayola crayon that popularized this exact hex value [4]. It sits firmly in the [[red]] family, tipped toward [[magenta]] rather than toward orange [3].
